paper_title: Evidence-Grounded Auditing of Identification Assumptions in Climate-Policy Causal Evaluations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Difference-in-differences (DID) studies are widely used to evaluate climate policy, but assessing the evidence supporting their identification assumptions remains challenging. We introduce ARGUS, a structured language-model pipeline that audits reported evidence against an eleven-dimension assumption-implication-evidence rubric and abstains when relevant evidence cannot be retrieved. We evaluate ARGUS using injected flaws, economics papers, and a small pilot with reconciled labels. On the 11-flaw benchmark, ARGUS detects 73% of planted flaws, compared with 18% for a keyword-based pipeline. Across 26 economics papers, ARGUS abstains on about 40% of paper-dimension assessments for lack of retrievable evidence. In a five-paper pilot with labels reconciled by two annotators, it assigns a higher risk level than the labels on 25 of the 33 assessments it completes. A rule fixed before the labels arrived removes most of this in-sample; weighted agreement stays low. ARGUS provides evidence-linked risk reports that localize potential weaknesses for expert review, without adjudicating causal claims. Code and data: https://github.com/yonghongzhang-io/ARGUS

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Difference-in-differences (DID) is widely used to evaluate climate and environmental policy, including carbon pricing, emissions-trading schemes, and emission standards. The credibility of these estimates depends on identification assumptions such as parallel trends, no anticipation, appropriate treatment of staggered adoption, and limited interference between units, each of which large body of methodological work has shown to be fragile (Bertrand et al., 2004; GoodmanBacon, 2021; Callaway and SantAnna, 2021; Sun and Abraham, 2021; de Chaisemartin and DHaultfœuille, 2020; Roth et al., 2023). These assumptions can be hard to assess in climate settings, where policies may overlap, be phased in over time, spill across administrative boundaries, and rely on modelled or remotely sensed outcomes (Appendix A). Where such estimates inform policy, causal conclusions built on weakly supported assumptions can mislead. Assessing an identifying assumption requires more than locating reported diagnostic. paper may present parallel trends over an event-study figure, leaving the reader to weigh the design, the pre-period estimates, the inference, and the policy timing before accepting the claim; the assessment has to be repeated for every assumption and every paper. This is one facet of broader concern with the reliability of empirical findings (Ioannidis, 2005; Silberzahn et al., 2018; Brodeur et al., 2020). We argue that identification credibility is auditable even when the true causal effect is not, building on the research-design tradition in applied econometrics (Angrist and Pischke, 2010; Athey and Imbens, 2017; Rambachan and Roth, 2023). is unobBecause the counterfactual served, ARGUS (named after Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed watchman) does not ask whether an estimated effect is true. Instead, it asks whether each identifying assumption is adequately supported by the evidence reported in the paper, and where that support is weakest. ARGUS represents DID study through an 11-dimension assumptionimplicationevidence rubric and uses retrieval-gated pipeline built on bounded, large language model (LLM) to retrieve relevant evidence, assess its adequacy, and produce an evidence-grounded risk report for expert review (Figure 1). Model agency is confined to scoped retrieval and assessment tasks behind fixed, deterministic control flow, unlike free-roaming agents whose control flow is model-decided (Yao et al., 2023); ARGUS flags potential weaknesses rather than adjudicating causal truth. threat into dimension whose supporting evidence can be checked in given paper (3). Evaluating such an auditor is difficult because the true policy effect is unobserved. We therefore use flaw injection as local ground truth: starting from supported study fixture, we introduce one known identification flaw and test whether ARGUS detects it, remains quiet on the clean version, and localizes the affected dimension. We complement this controlled evaluation with run over 26 corpus papers tagged DID and small diagnostic pilot with reconciled labels, used to identify calibration and applicability failures. Climate-policy evaluation motivates the rubric; the present evaluation uses synthetic environmental-policy fixtures and general-economics corpus, so performance on dedicated climate-policy corpus is untested. Contributions. We develop and evaluate rubric and pipeline for assessing the reported evidence behind DID identification assumptions, without access to the causal effect: 1. an operationalization: machine-auditable assumptionimplicationevidence rubric and bounded, evidence-grounded pipeline with explicit abstention (3); 2. an evaluation methodology: planted identification errors as local ground truth, with compute-graded and oracle ablations that locate the gain in per-dimension prompting and trace every synthetic omission miss to gate abstention (5); 3. diagnosis: on real papers, grounding limits coverage while over-severity limits agreement, and pre-specified rule derived on the same papers reduces the latter in-sample.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: DID identification and its threats. large econometrics literature formalizes when DID estimators fail under staggered timing and heterogeneous effects: two-way fixed effects use of already-treated units as controls (GoodmanBacon, 2021), negative weights (de Chaisemartin and DHaultfœuille, 2020), robust estimators (Callaway and SantAnna, 2021; Sun and Abraham, 2021), assumption and pre-trend surveys (Roth et al., 2023), and fragile inference under serial correlation (Bertrand et al., 2004). ARGUS adds no estimator: it operationalizes this literature as an auditable rubric, turning each known LLM causal reasoning and benchmarks. parallel line asks whether LLMs reason about causality. Benchmarks (CLadder (Jin et al., 2023), Corr2Cause (Jin et al., 2024), CausalBNBench (Zhou et al., 2026)) and analyses (Kıcıman et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Zeˇcevic et al., 2023) report mixed evidence: strong performance on some causal tasks, but models often reproduce causal language without reliable causal inference; few move toward applied settings and toward separating identification from estimation (Lee et al., 2025; Sawarni et al., 2026). ARGUS addresses different task: whether human papers identification assumptions are adequately evidenced. causal verdict is out of scope by design. Responsible AI for empirical research. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to research reliability: reproducibility checking, statistical-reporting validation, and AI-assisted review, motivated by wide analyst-driven result spreads (Silberzahn et al., 2018; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020) and specification searching in causal economics (Brodeur et al., 2020). LLMs are also used directly as evaluators and reviewers, judging model outputs (Zheng et al., 2023), giving feedback on research papers (Liang et al., 2024), and reviewing inside automated-science pipelines (Lu et al., 2024); these evaluators already produce ratings, pairwise preferences, and structured reviews. ARGUS applies an assumption-specific rubric to DID studies, links each dimension to in-paper evidence, and is measured against injected ground truth. ARGUS focuses on the evidence for identification credibility specifically (the assumptions supporting the causal interpretation) and issues no verdicts, producing evidence-grounded, humanreviewable reports that localize risk for the experts final call. Closest to our setting, CausalVerify (Zhang et al., 2026a) grounds evaluation in execution: it runs models generated estimation code against synthetic data and checks the recovered effect. That benchmark does not audit identification assumptions, which is the layer ARGUS takes up; we reuse its released corpus of economics papers and add dimension-level identification-risk annotation layer on top of it. Figure 1: Overview of ARGUS. Step 1 converts an empirical DID paper into an auditable structure using an 11dimension identification rubric. Step 2 retrieves dimension-specific evidence, assesses reported-evidence adequacy with bounded LLM audit module, and localizes risk in human-reviewable report. Step 3 uses labels from two annotators, reconciled by them, to evaluate audit severity and score pre-specified calibration rule offline; deployment requires only expert review of the report. Colours as in Figure 2: blue, deterministic steps; green, model calls; orange, human steps. Natural language processing for climate evidence. Natural language processing (NLP) systems for climate text verify claims against evidence (CLIMATE-FEVER (Diggelmann et al., 2020)), detect environmental claims (Stammbach et al., 2023), analyse corporate climate disclosures with traceable LLM answers (Ni et al., 2023), and tune models for faithful evidencebased question answering (Schimanski et al., 2024). These systems ground answers in documents; ARGUS extends document-grounded verification from claims to the identification argument of causal study, auditing whether reported evidence supports each assumption. Evaluation methodology and bounded agents. Our evaluation follows benchmarking lessons: holistic evaluation (Liang et al., 2023) over single number; dynamic, adversarial benchmarking (Kiela et al., 2021) (which inspires our controlled flaw injection); and the caution that operationalizing capability is non-neutral (Raji et al., 2021; Gebru et al., 2021) (6). closely related concern is that an agent benchmark can measure its harness rather than its model: Zhang et al. (2026b) show that fixed scaffold making the execution-critical decisions and scorer grading output shape mask each other, so repairing either alone leaves the ranking uninformative. Our abthey comlations apply related check inward: pare joint and per-dimension prompting, with and without retrieval and relevance gating, holding the model and rubric fixed (5.2). Where ReAct-style agents (Yao et al., 2023) choose their own action sequence, ARGUS fixes the order of retrieval and assessment and confines model calls to those two stages, trading autonomy for inspectability and evidence-traceability.

sections.title: 3 The ARGUS Framework
sections.content: 3.1 Identification rubric ARGUS decomposes DID study into eleven auditable dimensions of identification, design, inference, and reporting: parallel trends, no anticipation, staggered-timing handling, SUTVA (stable unit treatment value assumption, no interference) and spillovers, control-group construction, specification, inference, sample-period selection, concurrent policies, placebo/robustness, and data measurement. Each dimension is expressed as an assumption or design requirement (what must hold), testable implication (the diagnostic that should then be observable), and the evidence credible paper would report to support it. For carbon-pricing or emissions-trading evaluation, for instance, the parallel-trends dimension expects an event-study or pre-trend test with pre-period estimates near zero (an insignificant pre-trend alone can reflect low power; Roth, 2022), while noanticipation turns on the gap between schemes announcement and implementation dates. The rubric is declarative, stored in configuration file (identification_dimensions.yaml), so the audited dimensions are explicit and inspectable rather than buried in code. companion flaw taxonomy (4) maps each known identification threat one-to-one onto dimension, which both documents the rubrics coverage and supplies the perturbations used for evaluation. 3.2 Bounded LLM pipeline The audit runs fixed, deterministic sequence, decomposition extraction assessment localization report, shown in the top band of Figure 2. The stage order is written in code and never chosen by model. Decomposition instantiates the rubric for the paper at hand; extraction gathers, per dimension, the in-paper evidence relevant to that assumption; assessment evaluates each assumptionimplicationevidence chain and emits per-dimension risk judgement with rationale and cited evidence; localization aggregates these judgements into risk map that ranks the dimensions assigned the highest risk (ties broken by the fixed rubric order); and report renders transparent, evidence-grounded document for human reviewer. Model calls are confined to two stages, extraction and assessment. In the configuration evaluated in 5 they resolve, for each dimension, to fixed sequence: deterministic lexical retrieval over the papers sections and captions, one relevancegate call that labels each retrieved passage high, partial, or none, and, if at least one passage is kept, one adequacy call. If no passage is kept the dimension is scored unknown without an adequacy call; dimension with only partially relevant passages is still judged (Appendix D). Figures and tables enter only through their captions. The code also defines more general bounded loop for these two stages (a fixed tool set of evidence_search, figure_parse, and policy_lookup; hard step budget, max_steps; logged trace of every step and cited passage); the reported experiments run it with max_steps=1 and never invoke figure_parse or policy_lookup, and all other stages are plain orchestration with no model call. We therefore call the design bounded rather than agentic: the evaluated system is structured, dimension-scoped prompting over retrieved evidence with an explicit abstention path, not an open-ended agent. can inspect. It does not make model outputs identical: Appendix reports the variation observed across repeated runs. The expert sits at the end of the pipeline: ARGUS surfaces and localizes identification risk; the judgement itself stays with the human. 3.3 Output ARGUS emits studydimensionrisk triplets, each with an evidence-grounded rationale, alongside the human-readable report. In the evaluated prompts (Appendix E) low, medium, and high correspond approximately to retrieved evidence judged sufficient, partial, and missing or flawed; unknown is produced by the gate when no relevant passage is retained and reflects retrieval, not judgement about the paper. None of the four is verdict on the causal effect. This output shape keeps the system both auditable by human and measurable by the evaluation that follows.

sections.title: 4 Evaluation by Flaw Injection
sections.content: 4.1 Local ground truth without the counterfactual The defining difficulty in evaluating causalidentification auditor is that the quantity of ultimate interest (the true causal effect of carbon price, an emissions cap, or an emission standard) is never observed. We therefore do not attempt to certify that ARGUS recovers true effects. Instead we construct local ground truth by controlled perturbation. Beginning from short synthetic fixture, an environmental-policy DID study that reports supporting evidence on all eleven dimensions, we inject exactly one known flaw that targets single dimension, drawn from the flaw taxonomy (flaw_taxonomy.yaml; Appendix traces each flaw to the literature that names it). The target dimension is known by construction, and the expected response (risk of at least medium on that dimension) is defined by the rubric, without ever needing the true effect. The bottom band of Figure 2 shows the loop: the clean and injected versions are each audited, and three metrics are computed. Why bound the models role. Fixing the stage order makes the sequence of operations explicit and comparable across runs and keeps every judgement anchored to logged evidence human Detection: does the injected version raise risk on the targeted dimension to medium or above? (All reported results use this threshold.) Figure 2: ARGUS architecture. The top band is the audit pipeline, fixed deterministic sequence; model calls are confined to two stages (extraction and assessment). As evaluated, these resolve per dimension to fixed call sequence (lexical retrieval, one relevance-gate call, one adequacy call) with step budget of one and logged trace; the designed tools figure_parse and policy_lookup are not exercised (3.2). The bottom band shows the flaw-injection evaluation loop, which injects one known flaw, audits the clean and injected versions, and scores detection, false alarm, and localization against the injected flaw as local ground truth, never against the unobserved true effect. False alarm: does the clean version stay quiet on that dimension? Localization: is the targeted dimension the one the auditor flags most strongly? detector looks for. regression test fails if an injected paper contains the target dimensions predefined negative-signal phrases, so this phrase leakage cannot silently return; detection cannot come from matching those phrases. 4.2 Structural perturbation, not sentinels How flaw is injected is methodological choice that matters. naïve injector appends sentence that names the flaw: e.g. treated and control have non-zero pre-period coefficients with significant leads. If the detector then searches for exactly those phrases, detection becomes tautology: the injector plants the very string the detector matches on. In our initial implementation this produced detection rate of 1.000 inflated by phrase leakage. We replace this with structural perturbation of two kinds. Omission flaws remove the section, figure, or table that supplies the evidence the rubric specifies for dimension (e.g. deleting the placebo-robustness section or the balance table). They test sensitivity to missing reported support; they do not establish that the underlying assumption is violated. Commission flaws rewrite section to introduce stated design problem in prose intended to resemble how flawed paper would describe it (e.g. pooling all province-years in two-way fixed-effects regression under staggered policy timing), without the phrases the keyword

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: What ARGUS measures. measurement is only as good as the link between the construct and the task that operationalizes it (Jacobs and Wallach, 2021; Raji et al., 2021). ARGUS audits whether climate-policy studys identification assumptions are adequately supported by its reported evidence: reported-evidence adequacy is an operational proxy for identification credibility, not causal validity itself. Why climate policy. Climate-policy estimates inform governance, so confidently wrong credibility judgement has cost; ARGUS therefore abstains when its gate finds no relevant passage. Retrieval limits audit coverage. further gap is retrieving the relevant evidence. On the realpaper corpus it limits coverage, and in the pilot an assessor handed weakly relevant evidence usually rates the dimension high (20 of 22 weak-retrieval pilot cells), so ARGUS reports retrieval quality and an explicit unknown distinct from substantive high-risk judgement.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: The causal effect of climate policy is unobservable; whether studys reported evidence supports its identification assumptions can be assessed. ARGUS operationalizes that assessment with bounded, evidence-grounded pipeline, flaw injection as local ground truth, and reconciled pilot whose human labels evaluate the auditor and score pre-specified rule that reduces its overseverity in-sample; its value in expert review and on climate-policy papers is untested.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our human gold is pilot-scale: 5 papers and 55 cells from two annotators who reconciled their differences themselves, so the comparison is preliminary signal rather than calibrated benchmark; its labels are 84% medium, which makes exact agreement lenient and κ the more informative statistic. The gold is the reconciled judgement of two annotators, not of panel of DID methodologists; it has only two high cells; 23 of its 55 cells judge an analogue of the assumption because the design is not canonical DID; every agreement figure is conditional on the 33 cells ARGUS answered (it abstained on 22, on 19 of which both annotators found evidence); and constant medium label would out-score the calibrated system on exact agreement. The current scope is confined to difference-in-differences identification; whether the rubric-plus-injection methodology transfers to other quasi-experimental designs is untested. The rubric, flaw taxonomy, and injector are co-designed, so synthetic detection rates are best read as internal consistency under known threats rather than external generalization (Appendix traces each injected flaw to the literature that names it, so the threat catalogue is inherited while the injectors prose is ours); flaws authored by independent experts are future work. The benchmarks are small: at n=11 and n=33 no pairwise difference between architecture arms reaches significance under paired exact test, and the human-gold intervals are wide (Appendix G), so we report descriptive differences on these benchmarks; the samples do not establish population-level differences between the architecture variants. Those intervals and the cell-level paired tests also treat the 55 pilot cells as independent although they are nested in five papers, and the calibration rules were derived on the pilot they are scored on, so the calibration lift is an in-sample result whose size on unseen papers is untested. The parallel-trends criterion is likewise reporting check: ARGUS does not test whether pretrend test had the power to detect violation. The real corpus is general-economics stress test that contains no climate-policy evaluation in the narrow sense (Appendix H); climate-policy corpus run is the natural next test. Relatedly, flaw injection certifies the auditor against the injected threat on single dimension only and inherits the taxonomys blind spots, so we treat detection and localization as necessary rather than sufficient, pairing them with the false-alarm rate and the human-gold comparison. Evidence grounding limits coverage. ARGUS emits unknown only when the relevance gate finds no suitable passage; partial matches still reach the judge and can produce over-severe verdicts. Finally, ARGUS screens whether reported evidence supports studys identification assumptions and does not adjudicate the true causal effect, which is never observed. Its outputs surface risk for expert review and do not replace it.

sections.title: Rationale
sections.content: A.1 Why climate-policy DID is demanding audit setting Climate-policy evaluations can raise several identification challenges at once. Policy announcement, legal adoption, and actual implementation may occur at different dates, creating scope for anticipation. Carbon markets and environmental regulations may be introduced at different times across jurisdictions, so that heterogeneous and staggered treatment effects need to be handled. Emissions, investment, and production responses can spill across regional borders, challenging nointerference assumptions. Climate policies can overlap with industrial, energy, and air-pollution regulations, complicating the exclusion of concurrent interventions. Policy effects may emerge with long and heterogeneous lags. Emissions and environmental outcomes may be assembled from administrative, modelled, or remotely sensed sources whose measurement properties vary across places and time. These features do not make DID unique to climate policy; they motivate rubric that makes the evidence for each design choice explicit. A.2 Identification auditing and research reliability ARGUS addresses one component of broader research-reliability problem: published conclusions can vary with specification choices, undisclosed analytic flexibility, and researcher deIoannidis, freedom (Leamer, 1983; grees of 2005; Simmons et al., 2011; Gelman and Loken, 2014; Silberzahn et al., 2018; Brodeur et al., This is 2020; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020). the identification-credibility component of the broader research-design or credibility revolution program in applied econometrics (Angrist and Pischke, 2010; Athey and Imbens, 2017), which increasingly treats an assumption like parallel trends as matter of degree rather than binary (Rambachan and Roth, 2023; Roth, 2022). ARGUS does not attempt to audit every component of an empirical paper; it focuses on the assumptions that support causal interpretation. A.3 Why the pipeline is bounded Open-ended agents may choose different tools and reasoning paths across runs, making their outputs difficult to reproduce and compare. Large language models are increasingly used for evaluative and reviewing tasks (Zheng et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024), but as open-ended agents their reasoning traces are hard to audit. ARGUS instead fixes the pipeline order in code and confines model-driven decisions to evidence retrieval and adequacy assessment. Each model call operates under fixed tool set, hard step budget, and logged trace. This design trades autonomy for inspectability and controlled evaluation under flaw injection; it fixes the sequence of operations, not the models outputs.

sections.title: D Retrieval Details
sections.content: The only corpus queried is the paper under audit; there is no external corpus and no embedding index. Papers are ingested through light markdown convention (## section headings plus @figure/@table caption lines), and the searchable blocks are the title, abstract, each section, and each figure or table caption. On the LLM path retrieval is section-level and lexical: each dimension has fixed query pack of 1119 distinct terms (e.g. pre-trend, event study, lead coefficients for parallel trends), block scores by the summed frequency of its matched terms, and the top k=4 blocks are kept, each truncated to 2,000 characters. The relevance gate sees the first 1,200 characters of each candidate and labels it high, partial, or none; retrieval quality is good if any candidate is high, weak if only partial candidates remain, and failed otherwise. failed dimension is scored unknown without an adequacy call; weak and good dimensions pass the kept blocks, in full, to the adequacy judge together with the rubrics assumption, implication, and expected evidence. The keyword baseline instead searches paragraph chunks capped at 900 characters (sentence-split when longer) with single query string and top k=5, scoring positive and retrieval quality failed (22) weak (22) good (11) unknown 22 0 0 high medium low 0 0 0 2 1 5 0 20 5 negative sentinel phrases. With max_steps=1 there is no iterative exploration, so breadth is the top-k cap and depth is one round. Chunk size, k, and embedding retrieval were not swept. The oracle-retrieval arm of 5.2 is diagnostic comparison in which the target section is supplied directly and the gate is bypassed; it is not formal upper bound on retrieval performance. Table 7 shows how the gates three outcomes map to risk on the pilot-gold cells, the mechanism behind the fixture/real-paper asymmetry of 5.3.
